Executive summary  
After seven years of a devastating civil war, which ended in 1997, Liberia is still faced with the challenges of reconciliation, peace building, reconstruction and recovery. The incidence of poverty remains extremely high with 76.2% of the population living below the poverty line of US$ 1 per day, with severe poverty estimated at 52%. The current elected government of Liberia installed in 1997 has not been able to generate the required resources domestically and internationally to revive the economy to its pre-war level. The objectives of the national Five-year Medium Term Plan for Reconstruction and Development (MTP), prepared with UNDP’s assistance, are to consolidate peace, reinforce the democratization process, and strengthen the mechanism for conflict prevention, good governance, macroeconomic reforms, socio-economic development and poverty reduction. 
All dimensions of human development indicated in the United Nations Common Country Assessment (CCA) are low. Liberia is among the most food insecure countries with 35% of the population undernourished. With a population of 2.7 million, life expectancy is recorded at 47.7 years. Under-five mortality is 194 per 1000 with maternal mortality at 578/100 000 live births. HIV/AIDS prevalence has increased to 8.2% with an upward trend. About 75% of the population lack access to primary health care and safe drinking water. The literacy rate is only at 33% (compared to 58% for Sub Saharan Africa) with high gender disparities (40% for male and 26% for female). 
Furthermore, since 1999, the outlook for durable peace and security has been dampened by sporadic fighting with dissidents in the northern county of Lofa. In 2002, the conflict has spread to five counties causing nationwide insecurity. The immediate backdrop to the current crisis can be traced to portions of the Abuja Peace agreement not implemented, under which elections were held following the disarmament of the factions in 1997. The Disarmament, Demobilization and Reintegration (DDR) process was not completed and remobilization has occurred. The expansion of State militias and security forces contributes further to the gun culture and insecurity across Liberia. 
The renewed hostilities have resulted in significant displacements of populations both internally and externally.  The gains that have been made in the recovery and resettlement of displaced people and refugees between 1997 and 2000 are being reversed by a new humanitarian crisis. Presently, over 100,000 people are internally displaced due to the on going fighting between the dissident and government forces. There is equally, a growing number of Liberian refugees in neighboring countries. This continuous instability in Liberia is creating a perpetual dependency syndrome, which has damaging consequences for the future development of the country. Cumulatively, about 20% of the Liberian population depended on humanitarian assistance in 2001. 
In respect to the rehabilitation and reconstruction needs of Liberia, the response of the international community has slacked since the last donor conference organized in Paris, in April 1998. Between 1997 and 1999, development assistance has declined by 72 %. In addition, since May 2001 the country is under selective sanctions imposed by the Security Council for allegedly supporting the Revolutionary United Front (RUF) of Sierra Leone in diamonds and arms smuggling in Sierra Leone. Donors have been reluctant to support development activities, owing to donor fatigue in general and specific concerns about good governance, human rights and respect of the rule of law. UN Agencies, EU and USAID have maintained their assistance in the areas of social services, food security, governance and humanitarian services. The World Bank and the IMF are not present in Liberia, due to government’s lack of commitment to fiscal and structural reforms. 
The consolidation of peace remains the most urgent challenge facing Liberia. The root causes of the conflict identified as weak economic management, social inequalities and ethnic polarization remain to a great extent unresolved. The spiral of armed conflict, weak governance and poverty has constituted a vicious cycle that represents a great challenge for peace-building and progress towards recovery and long term sustainable development. 
The UN System over all objective is to contribute to the fulfillment of both humanitarian and developmental objectives as spelled out in the Medium Term Plan. The United Nations Agencies have adopted a comprehensive approach to peace building including the transition from relief to sustainable recovery. The complexity of the Liberian situation still requires the building up of synergies between humanitarian and development efforts. This strategy is predicated on the urgent need to put in place the building blocks for the effective transition from dependence on humanitarian relief to longer-term sustainable recovery. These building blocks also constitute a foundational support for the inclusive and durable peace process in Liberia. 
In view of the above-mentioned goals and the challenges of the current country context, United Nations assistance is geared towards (I) resolving the conflict and building sustainable peace, through supporting community rehabilitation and reconciliation including reintegration of refugees and internally displaced persons (II) building institutional capacity for good governance and economic management, (III), improving food security, livelihood opportunities and nutrition (IV) improving health sector services and fighting HIV/AIDS and other infectious diseases. Special attention will be given to targeting support to vulnerable groups (women and children) as well as enhancing the role of women and the youth in conflict resolution and peace building.
	The UN System will work together to achieve the goals of sustainable peace and recovery in Liberia. Collaborative programming among the UN agencies encompasses options of parallel and joint programming. The strategic aim of such arrangements is to enhance development impact through the synergistic combination of inputs from two or more UN agencies. UN agencies have selected a number of areas where they will carry out joint assessment, and design collaborative programmes consisting of shared objectives, actions and timeframes with a clear delineation of responsibilities. Among them peace education and human rights, reintegration of ex-combatants, repatriation, resettlement and reintegration of war affected populations, protection, nutrition, gender equity and empowerment, immunization, HIV/AIDS, malaria.  
Thematic groups will be a critical mechanism to plan, monitor and carry out initiatives proposed in the UNDAF, including proposals for parallel or joint programming. The implementation of the UNDAF will support the government in aid coordination. The UN Country Team will hold a mid-term review of the UNDAF with the government and other development partners to review the achievement of the objectives, including the quality of partnership and collaborative programming. At the end of the UNDAF cycle, the UN Country Team will organize an evaluation of the UNDAF. In particular, the periodic reviews of the UNDAF will be an opportunity to bring together a wide range of partners to discuss major development issues for the country. The follow-up of the UNDAF shall also provide an opportunity to secure additional resources in support of national needs and priorities.
Part I. Rationale of the UNDAF 
UN Reform and the UNDAF
In 1997, the UN Secretary General launched a programme for reform to improve the development work of the United Nations. One major reform proposal was the United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) intended to bring greater coherence to the United Nations development operations at the country level. 
In light of Liberia’s complex development situation, the standard framework for the UNDAF did not seem appropriate. The UNCT (includes the UN Office for Peace Building in Liberia- UNOL)  therefore decided to opt for a "modified UNDAF", that would bring together humanitarian assistance and development in a peace-building continuum. 
Modified UNDAFs have been used in a number of crisis/post-conflict countries in which the UN Country Team felt that full fledged CCAs and UNDAFs were not relevant considering the country context and that what was needed was a more comprehensive and flexible framework that linked relief, development and peace-building.  
 The substantive issues addressed by the modified UNDAF are guided by the Common Country Assessment (CCA), the Consolidated Appeal Process on humanitarian assistance (CAP) and the national Medium Term Plan (MTP). The UNCT is in the process of preparing a draft Peacebuilding Strategy for Liberia, that will be grounded in the modified UNDAF.
UNDAF in Liberia 
The national development strategy, as set out in the Medium Term Plan (MTP) focuses on reconciliation and consolidation of peace, security and governance, reintegration and resettlement, public sector effectiveness and transparency, private sector development, job creation and growth, rehabilitation of basic social services, and reconstruction of statistics and the database. The over-arching theme of this strategy is poverty reduction in a context of transition to sustainable recovery.
The UNDAF is developed to contribute to the above goal of the Government, building on on-going programmes dealing with humanitarian assistance, return and reintegration of refugees and internally displaced persons, transition to sustainable recovery, conflict resolution, strengthened governance, food security, reproductive health, child protection, survival and development and the empowerment of women as well as environmental sustainability. In all this, the modified UNDAF is designed to assist the government in creating the enabling environment within which the country would work towards meeting the Millennium Development Goals.
Peace, security, human rights and development are recognized as interdependant conditions for recovery in Liberia. The objective of the modified UNDAF is to define a strategic path that will accelerate the national recovery and reconstruction process and institutionalize an approach linking peace-building and development. 
Part II. Development Context: Poverty and Conflict nexus in Liberia 
Background
The 2003-2005 modified United Nations Development Framework (UNDAF) for Liberia is informed by the current state of economic development as well as conflicts within the Mano River Basin. 
After seven years of a devastating civil war, which caused over 200 000 deaths and displaced up to 80% of the total population of 2.5 million, Liberia is still faced with the challenges of reconciliation, peace building, reconstruction and recovery. The newly elected government installed in 1997, saddled with an enormous national debt burden of US$2.8 billion has not been able to generate the required resources domestically and internationally to revive the economy to its pre-war level. After five years of transition, GDP remains below 50% of its pre war level; the unemployment rate in the formal sector is approximately 85%. In addition to a severe decline in international aid, since May 2001 the country is under selective sanctions imposed by the Security Council for allegedly supporting the Revolutionary United Front (RUF) of Sierra Leone in diamonds and arms smuggling, which has increasingly adversely affected foreign investment and donor confidence.
Furthermore, the outlook for durable peace and security has been dampened by sporadic fighting with dissidents in the northern county of Lofa, resulting in significant new displacements of populations. In early 2002, the conflict has spread to five counties i.e. one third of the country, causing nationwide insecurity as thousands have been further displaced and security forces deployed across the country. An estimate of 100,000 displaced population require humanitarian assistance for their survival in 2002.
Despite these trends, there are ongoing efforts aimed at looking for possibilities to initiate a meaningful process of national reconciliation that would pave the way for elections scheduled for October 2003. This is a critical condition for creating a conducive environment for stability and effective support to ongoing efforts to move from a dependence on humanitarian relief toward reintegration and recovery. 
In 2001, the Liberian government embarked on the preparation of a five-year Medium Term Plan for Reconstruction and Development (MTP) to succeed the National Reconstruction Programme (NRP) that was prepared just after the end of the hostilities in 1997. 
Sub-regional dimension of the conflict in Liberia
The outbreak of civil war in Liberia in 1989 signaled the beginning of a major sub-regional crisis. In 1991, the conflict spread to Sierra Leone as the Revolutionary United Front (RUF) launched an incursion in Sierra Leone that resulted in the displacement of at least 70% of the country's 4.5 million citizens. As violence escalated in Sierra Leone and Liberia, Guinea and Ivory Coast became the main hosts of the refugee populations. Since then, there have been consistent accusations and counter accusations among the three countries of the Mano River Union (Liberia, Guinea and Sierra Leone) of either cross border attacks or armed support to dissidents. 
Despite the improved prospects for peace in Sierra Leone, the situation within the Mano River basin remains fragile. The conflict dynamics are threatening political stability within the broader ECOWAS sub region. The flows of refugees are creating new security problems and putting additional pressure on the already fragile economies and limited infrastructures of the host countries. 
Nevertheless, the resumption of peace negotiations between the three Mano River Union (MRU) countries brings some hope of stabilization within the region. After a long stalemate following the decision to revilitise the MRU institutions in 2000, the three Heads of State of Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone met again in February 2002 in Rabat, Morocco and reaffirmed their determination to rein in cross-border incursions which have been the major cause of conflict in the sub-region. 
Poverty in Liberia
Poverty is a multi-dimensional phenomenon with economic, social and political ramifications. Governance, management of natural resources, the state of infrastructures, level of education, population growth, gender disparities are determinants of poverty in Liberia. 
Poverty is manifested by the lack of adequate basic means and/or necessities of life: food, shelter, clothing, safe drinking water, health services, sanitary facilities, education and energy, as well as lack of free speech, information, assembly and participation. Among all, hunger is the most critical manifestation of poverty in Liberia. 
Liberia is classified as one of the least developed and most poverty stricken countries, with a ranking 174 out of 175 on the human development index. The incidence of poverty in Liberia is wide spread. Three-fourths (76%) of the population live under the poverty line of less than US$1.00 per day, with 52% living in extreme poverty, on less than US$0.50 per day. Liberia is among the most food insecure countries with 35% of the population undernourished. Life expectancy is recorded at 47.7 years. Child mortality is 194 per 1000, with maternal mortality at 578/100 000 live births. An estimated 75% of the population lack access to primary health care and safe drinking water. HIV/AIDS prevalence has increased to 8.2% with an upward trend. The literacy rate is only at 33% (compared to 58% for Sub Saharan Africa) with high gender disparities (50% for male and 24% for female).
Box 2. Who are the poor ? 
Poverty in Liberia is primarily a rural phenomenon. More than half the people live in rural areas and 86.3% of rural households are poor and 64% live in severe poverty. However still the majority of Liberia's urban population falls below the poverty line (50.6 % in the capital Monrovia). The poor are most likely found in a male-headed household engaged in farming as the main source of livelihood.  While the poor will most likely be uneducated and illiterate, more and more people with education are becoming poor because of unemployment. 
Poverty in Liberia is undermining sustainable human development and constitutes a threat to social and political stability. Since the causes of poverty are multiple, an integrated and holistic, approach to alleviating it will be required.
Conflicts in Liberia 
Internal conflicts, civil war and cross border attacks into Liberia have disrupted political, social, and economic development in Liberia since the 1980s.  The various manifestations of poor governance and poverty were instrumental in precipitating political tensions and ethnic polarization that led to the civil war. The military rule (1980- 1985) further exacerbated political, ethnic tensions and confidence crises, crowding out investments and capital. Unemployment rate rose to over 50%. The transformation of the military regime in 1985 to a civilian one, through an election characterized by rigging was the trigger of the events that would lead to the outbreak of a civil war in 1989. Although the civil war officially ended in 1996, following 13 peace agreements under the auspices of the ECOWAS and the UN, social, political and ethnic tensions as well as societal polarization still persist. 
Many opposition leaders and former warring faction heads have fled into exile, while others are alleged to be supporting dissident groups who have been since 1999 to overthrow the government. Although the country is not yet engulfed in the renewed wave of fighting, this “no peace no war” situation has defined the elusiveness of lasting peace and sustainable recovery in Liberia for almost two decades. 
The Imperative of Peace Building
The vicious circle of armed conflict, high level of unemployment, particularly among youths, weak governance including specifically grave concerns over the management of the exploitation of natural resources, have exacerbated the spiral of violence and poverty and hindered conflict resolution and sustained recovery.  The pernicious nature of the relationship between poverty and armed conflict following almost 20 years of war has resulted in dislocated populations and fractured communities. Poor governance has been a critical factor in Liberia manifesting itself in several forms: weak economic accountability, disrespect of the rule of law, questions of human rights etc. Poverty, conflict, and underdevelopment conspire and create a “zero-sum” game in which sustainable recovery could be ultimately compromised.
Political stability in Liberia is thus a social, economic and political imperative. It constitutes the foundation for Liberia’s post-war rehabilitation and reconstruction as well as her economic recovery and growth. It will require both the promotion of peace making and peace building in order to ensure that there is genuine national reconciliation and the required capacity to carry through the process of sustainable recovery. 
UN Response: UNDAF scope and focus
To progress towards the achievement of the Millennium Development Goals, the C.C.A. and the national Medium Term Plan have identified the key development challenges in Liberia as follows: fragile peace and the induced humanitarian crisis, residual governance problems with respect to human rights and the rule of law, weak capacities in economic management and agriculture planning, the destruction of social and economic infrastructures, illiteracy and the high vulnerability of the population to infectious diseases including HIV/AIDS and malaria. As indicated above, national reconciliation and the consolidation of peace remains the most urgent challenge facing Liberia. The root causes of the conflict identified as weak economic management, social inequalities and ethnic polarization remain to a great extent unresolved.

Accordingly, the modified UNDAF focuses on four priority thematic areas and three cross cutting issues for intervention and support. The thematic areas are: (i) conflict resolution and peace building (ii) good governance; (iii) food security and nutrition (iv) reproductive health, combating HIV/AIDS, malaria and other prevalent diseases. The cross cutting issues are: (i) gender; (ii) child protection and development; and (iii) environmental and natural resource management.

THEME 1 	CONFLICT RESOLUTION AND PEACE BUILDING 
Goal:	to seek resolution of the present armed conflict and to initiate a peace process that addresses the root causes of conflict and the resulting humanitarian situation.
Context
The seven-year conflict left communities disintegrated, families dispossed, and individuals traumatized. After five years of transition and economic stagnation, populations are still very vulnerable.  Basic social services are not operational in the major part of the country, due to the destruction of most social infrastructures (schools, clinics) and roads and bridges during the civil war. Estimates indicates that 60% of the schools were destroyed, access to safe water supply reduced to 26%, access to health service to 25% (the percentage of household within 2 hours of health facility is 80%). The absence of functioning social services in rural areas may hamper the revival process of the fractured communities as well as the reintegration process of IDPs and returnees. The decline in the delivery of social services also serves as disincentive for rural dwellers, particularly farmers, and has contributed to the migration to urban areas.
For most of 2001, dissident incursions allegedly mounted by the Liberians United for Reconciliation and Democracy (LURD) has worsened the security concerns. In 2002, the spreading of the fighting to five counties, notably to the second city of the country, Gbarnga, and to the vicinity of the capital, Monrovia, has heightened the tension. 
The gains made in the resettlement and reintegration of displaced people and refugees between 1997 and 2000 are being reversed by a new humanitarian crisis. The spread of the fighting between Government forces and dissidents has resulted in a significant increase in IDP caseload, officially estimated to be 100,000 in 2002 compared to a planning figure of 30,000 in 2001. In addition, an estimated population of 200,000 IDPs and refugees are believed to remain in conflict areas, not accessible to humanitarian workers. A population of about 35,000 refugees from Sierra Leone receives humanitarian and protection assistance from UNHCR. Concurrently, the number of Liberian refugees who have fled to neighboring Sierra Leone has topped the 25,000 while 16,000 have fled to Guinea and 10,000 to Ivory Coast in mid 2002. The Liberia Refugee Repatriation and Resettlement Commission (LRRRC) does not have the capacity nor the financial means to effectively play its coordination and monitoring role. The presence of UNHCR, the establishment of the OCHA office and the Humanitarian Coordinator have significantly enhanced the coordination of humanitarian support.
Further displacement of populations is likely to have far reaching consequences on the survival economy of the already impoverished rural communities throughout the country. It is all the more necessary to address the need for a wide range of community-based relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction assistance to help the poorest and most vulnerable communities to cope with additional pressure from the influx of IDPs. The further displacement and increase of IDPs, in particular the massive influx of IDPs around the capital is a factor of tension in the Liberian society. There is thus an urgent need to work towards achieving durable peace and reconciliation among all Liberians. The entire spectrum of peace making and peace building, should be vigorously pursued.
Five years after democratic elections, the political landscape remains uncertain, especially as the country moves towards general elections in 2003. The rule of law and respect for human rights are critical challenges. In 2002, some steps have been taken by the Government to initiate a process of national reconciliation such as the presidential amnesty for some political opponents, in furtherance of confidence-building, and the preparation of a National Reconciliation Conference in Liberia scheduled for July 2002. ECOWAS has continued to intensify its effort in consolidating peace in the sub-region and has been instrumental in renewing the dialogue between the opposition and the government with active support from civil society. In March 2002, under the auspices of ECOWAS, in Abuja, Nigeria, government representatives have engaged in dialogue with civil society organizations and opposition leaders, including those in the diaspora. 
Civil Society groups and in particular the Mano River Women Peace Network (MARWOPNET) have played a pivotal role in fostering peace within the Mano River Union, which culminated with the Summit of the Heads of State of Liberia, Sierra Leone and Guinea in February 2002 in Rabat under the auspices of King Mohamed V of Morocco. In furtherance to the Rabat Summit, it was decided to revive the Mano River Union Joint Security Committee, which comprises the Ministers of Defense of the three countries. The MRU Foreign Ministers, meeting in Agadir in April 2002, agreed on the deployment of joint border security and confidence building units along the borders of the Mano River Basin in a determined bid to rein in cross-border incursions which have been the major cause of conflict in the sub-region. 
The fact that Liberian armed forces are still to be restructured remains a matter of concern. The co-existence of several legally established units and a number of special military or paramilitary groups within the Liberian armed forces, most of them being under paid, with no unity of command, is not conducive to the strengthening of the security environment. The Demobilization, Restruturing and Reintegration process initiated by ECOMOG was not seen through completion and many of the core ex-combatants have been reintegrated into the renewed security apparatus. In late 2000, a commission to downsize and restructure the army was established by the government. The demobilization, restructuring, and re-training of the national army and the police, is a necessary condition to attain sustainable peace and security, the restoration of the respect for human rights and the rule of law in Liberia. 
The UN System will develop and implement a post conflict strategy to consolidate and sustain peace that embraces a series of activities: political, humanitarian and development related. The Security Council, in a statement of 20 February 2001, recognized that  "peace building is aimed at preventing the outbreak, the recurrence or continuation of armed conflict and therefore encompass a wide range of political developmental, humanitarian and human rights programmes and mechanisms. These actions should focus on fostering sustainable institutions and processes in areas such as sustainable development, the eradication of poverty and inequalities, transparent and accountable governance, the promotion of democracy, respect for human rights and the rule of law and the promotion of a culture of peace and non violence."  This strategy will address reconciliation and recovery through an approach that supports sustainable reintegration of displaced persons primarily through the restoration of basic social services, confidence building related processes as well as the creation of job opportunities and means of sustainable livelihoods. 
KEY CHALLENGES
The key challenges for conflict resolution and peace building in the country are the initiation of a genuine reconciliation at the national and community levels, the rebuilding of fractured communities and the reintegration of displaced populations, and the restoration of a security environment conducive for human development. 
UN RESPONSE
The UN system has over the years contributed substantially to the peace process in Liberia. It directly supported ECOWAS in bringing the warring parties to a negotiated settlement that led to the 1997 presidential and general elections. The Secretary-General has designated a Special Representative in Liberia to work with the government to consolidate Liberia’s fragile peace. 
The United Nations Office for Peace Building (UNOL), as well as UNDP, UNFPA and UNICEF, have been supporting the reconciliation process and the restoration of sustainable peace in the region, notably through the Mano River Women’s Peace Network. UNOL worked closely with ECOWAS and UNAMSIL as well as with civil society organizations to support the Liberian Government to contribute to the peace process in Sierra Leone. UNOL and the UN agencies contributed significantly to creating awareness on issues of respect for the rule of law and human rights. UNOL and UNDP supported the government to demobilize and restructure the security forces. 
The UN System, in particular WFP, UNHCR, UNICEF, WHO, UNFPA, FAO have endeavored to respond to the humanitarian needs of the IDPs and refugees while UNDP, FAO, UNICEF have been working to strengthen the coping mechanisms of the fractured communities. The UN System has focused its humanitarian and community revival efforts on the most vulnerable groups.
Objective 1:	strengthened political dialogue at national and sub-regional level 
The UN system will support political dialogue, reconciliation, peace education and confidence building as means of resolving the armed conflict and attaining durable peace in Liberia. The UN’s efforts in this area shall entail support for: (i) facilitating the dialogue processes; and (ii) supporting consultative processes and peace summits of ECOWAS and Mano River countries (iii) supporting peace education and confidence building among the Liberian society. 
The United Nations System will continue to support the national reconciliation process, in fostering confidence building and dialogue among the Liberian society, including opposition leaders. UNOL will continue to be involved in the preparation of a National Reconciliation Conference, which shall bring together all of Liberia’s political groupings both in and out of the country, and shall be a major undertaking aimed at identifying the immediate and underlying causes of Liberia’s conflict prone situation and, develop a framework in which these shortcomings shall be addressed.
Given the regional dimensions of the conflict, the UN shall support political dialogues and reconciliation consultations among the three Mano River governments and peoples. The efforts already started by women’s groups, religious’ groups, youths’ groups, and other civil society organizations shall be supported. Particularly, the UN shall support consultative meetings and summits of Mano River leaders and ECOWAS. The involvement of the Office of the Secretary General will be considered to strengthen and give credence to agreements emanating from negotiations talks. 
The UN system will play its advocacy role on peace education and confidence building. The culture of violence and impunity has to be debased. The traditional practices of information sharing, sense of community, collective responsibility and accountability need to be restored. The UN shall support civic education to prepare the ground for participative political and decision making process. The participation of local communities in confidence building and peace education shall be encouraged. Local ownership of conflicts and their resolutions are essential to the achievement of durable peace. The United Nations shall support civil society organizations in networking and building capacity in advocacy for peace. Particularly, meaningful efforts of women and youth groups as well as professional bodies in these areas shall be supported.
Proposed activities: 
Support consultative process at sub-regional and regional levels
Facilitate the dialogue process between Government, civil society and opposition leaders
Strengthen the capacity of CBOs involved in peace building and reconciliation 
Develop a Peace Education framework 
Promote tolerance, coexistence, reconciliation through peace education campaign at the national and community level (training of teachers, sensitization of community leaders)
Indicators:
Cease-fire agreement is concluded and hostilities ended
Consultations held at community, national and regional levels
Capacity of CBOs strengthened, peace campaigns conducted
Peace education framework produced and 
Inclusion of public education in the curriculum / number of teachers trained on peace education
Partnership Strategy
UNOL, UNDP, UNESCO, UNICEF, UNHCR
UNOL will spearhead the dialoguing process, identify the conflicting parties and initiate mediation among them, in collaboration with ECOWAS, OAU and other relevant organizations. UNOL will facilitate the sub-regional consultative process leading to peace summits in the Mano River Union and ECOWAS. UNOL will work with the Government and CBOS/CSOs in planning a national reconciliation conference. UNDP, UNICEF and UNHCR will take leadership on the peace education campaign at the grassroots levels. UNDP, UNICEF, UNOL will work together to develop a peace education framework.
Objective 2:	strengthened social cohesion through relief, reintegration and confidence building of war-affected populations (IDPs, refugees, returnees, host communities)
The UN System will continue to follow a dual approach to address the needs of the displaced populations and the refugees whilst strengthening the capacity of the host populations and other vulnerable communities in rural Liberia. The UN System will address reconciliation and recovery through a community-based approach that supports confidence-building processes through the rehabilitation of social infrastructures and the creation of job opportunities and means of sustainable livelihoods. The UN’s efforts in this area shall entail support for: (i) addressing the basic humanitarian needs of the IDPs and refugees (ii) supporting reintegration and resettlement processes of IDPs and returnees and the repatriation of refugees (iii) restoring basic social infrastructures and providing sustainable livelihood opportunities to revive communities. 
WFP emergency programme will continue to provide monthly food rations to refugees and internally displaced, as well as therapeutic feeding and school feeding in IDP and refugee camps and to the most vulnerable populations. UNICEF, WHO, UNFPA will focus their assistance on immunization, delivery of essential drugs, provision of safe drinking water and sanitation, as well as provision of emergency education in life skills, such as reproductive health and prevention and control of STDs and HIV/AIDS. On the issue of protection of vulnerable groups, UNDP, UNICEF, UNHCR and OCHA will advocate for strengthened child protection and will provide legal and trauma healing services for abused women and children in IDP and refugee camps. Humanitarian assistance shall also include tracing and family reunification programs for children. 
The UN system will support the development and implementation of programs, which will resettle and reintegrate IDPs and returnees into their communities of origin. For the Sierra Leonean population that took refuge in Liberia, UNHCR will continue a programme of voluntary repatriation to Sierra Leone including transportation and resettlement packages. The Reintegration and Resettlement program will target internally displaced persons and Liberian returnees. The needs to be attended shall include transportation, food and the recommencement of agricultural production, rural shelters construction, health and reproductive care provision, and water and sanitation services. The Volontary Repatriation, and Reintegration and Resettlement Programme will be coordinated by UNHCR and OCHA respectively, with UNDP, UNICEF, WHO, UNFPA and FAO support for the transition between return and resettlement. The program shall seek to address the related challenges of training, land tenure and start-up economic support.

THEME 2:	GOOD GOVERNANCE
Goal: to create an enabling environment for sustainable human development
Good governance remains a key development challenge in Liberia.  There is a consensus amongst Liberians that policies and practices avariance with tenets of good governance contributed to the Liberian civil war (1998-1996). For over a century, following the founding of Liberia, successive governments in Liberia excluded a segment of the population of the country from participating in the decision making process and the management and use of national resources.
The civil war led to collapse of almost all governance institutions, human rights and the rule of law, including the Judiciary, the police and other security forces.
In spite of the official cessation of hostilities and the inauguration of a government in 1997, following presidential and legislature elections, little has been done to reverse the exclusionary policies of the past, institutionalize popular participation, sustainable peace, and accountability and transparency in the management of national resources. National debt has become unsustainable at more than 20% of GDP and 80% of export earnings.  
KEY CHALLENGES
The restoration of peace and the institutions of governance are the single most imperative condition for recovery and development in Liberia.  The critical governance concerns are as follows:
Create an enabling environment conducive for free and fair elections 
Revitalize governance institutions, respect of human rights and the rule of law; 
Build capacity of public accountability for exploitation of natural resources and expenditures management 
Restore the statistical and planning system

The main goal is to strengthen and enhance a pluralistic, and participatory democracy, and to uphold the principles and practices of good governance so as to ensure durable peace, stability, and sustainable human development.

THEME  3:	FOOD SECURITY AND NUTRITION 
Goal : to improve living conditions of the poor and to create opportunities for sustainable livelihoods
Food security involves the availability, accessibility and affordability of adequate quantities of nutritious foods. Food security is worsening in Liberia and hunger and malnutrition are pervasive. The destructive effects of the seven-year (1989-1996) civil war damaged the agricultural sector, resulting in the displacement of the farming population, loss of lives and properties, including infrastructure, tools and planting materials; Health, educational, water and sanitation facilities were also damaged, thereby reducing the delivery of social services needed by rural dwellers. Food production, rice production in particular, is declining due to the resumption of hostilities in the northwestern part of the country, which are widely regarded as the ‘bread basket’ of the country. 
The incidence of food insecurity and poverty is severe in the rural areas. More than half the population live in rural areas, with farming as their main source of livelihood. 86.3% of rural households are poor and 64% live in severe poverty. The production of the traditional subsistent farms is very low and seasonal with few or no cash transactions. 
The agriculture sector (excluding forestry) accounted for 59% of GDP in 2001 and occupy 70% of the Labor force. It is still characterized by the use of traditional farming practices, lack of inputs, lack of credit facilities, access roads and price incentives. In addition, the development of the agriculture sector is constrained by continuous nation-wide insecurity. The progress made in the production of the food crops (rice and cassava) which had reached 70% of pre-war level in 1999 (although self sufficiency only stood at 65% of the national requirements in the 80's) is threatened by the new displacement of the farming population from the most productive regions of the country. Food production is also suffering from the lack of appropriate extension services and post-harvest technologies.  There is no comprehensive policy for the development of the agriculture sector. 
Encouraging the huge labor force of the rural areas to effectively participate in the growth of the economy poses the challenge to expand the access of the rural farmers to land, credit, infrastructure (markets & roads)  and the delivery of extension services for the promotion and dissemination of improved seed varieties and farming technology.  The development of rural Liberia needs the strong provision and support of rural infrastructure as well as making technological innovations accessible to the rural farmers. Access to better and improved infrastructure can lead to increased productivity in the rural areas and enhance strong market linkages. 
Malnutrition is prevalent, especially among children and mothers in the rural areas. Liberia falls in the group of countries that have more than 35% of its population undernourished. There is inadequate knowledge about proper nutritional practices and the need to reduce micronutrient deficiencies. Under-nutrition is widespread with about 39% of children under five years of age stunted, 6% thin and 26 % underweight. There is prevalence of iron deficiency anemia among children and pregnant women.
Rice is the main staple food in Liberia, and it accounts for about 80 percent of daily food intake in the average household.  Food sufficiency in Liberia is therefore broadly equated with ‘rice availability’ in sufficient quantity to meet daily dietary needs.  Households that fall short of the daily minimum rice intake are generally regarded as food poor, even when caloric intake from non-rice sources is above the survival minimum of 1,500 kcal. Improving the nutritional levels in Liberia will require improvement in the household food security situation. In this regard, raising the incomes of the poor farmers is a priority. 
KEY CHALLENGES
The key challenges to be addressed during the UNDAF period are as follows:
Creating an enabling environment for food production
Going beyond self subsistence farming to increase incomes generated from the agricultural sector and therefore improve the nutrition levels of the poor, especially of women and children

THEME  4:	REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH, COMBATING HIV/AIDS, MALARIA AND OTHER DISEASES
Goal: to improve life expectancy and to contain the prevalence of HIV/AIDS and other infectious diseases
The vulnerability of the Liberian population to health hazards is an impedious to recovery and development. HIV/AIDS , Malaria and other infectious diseases such as tuberculosis are main causes of death. In addition, the lack of control on sexual/reproductive health continue to hamper balanced socio-economic development and population growth.
With a population of 2.7 million, life expectancy is recorded at 47.7 years. The estimated population growth rate of 2.4%, although a decline from the 3.4% recorded in 1984, is still one of the highest in the world. The population is young, with approximately 48% being under 15 years which induces a high age-dependency burden. 
Pervasive poverty, the disruption of family structures and the profound erosion of cultural and societal values contribute to the high teen-age pregnancies. The reproductive sex life begins at a very early age. The acceptance of family planning is limited in Liberia. The average woman bears a little over six children during her child- bearing period (15-40 years).  Fertility is lower in the urban areas, and amongst women with a minimum high school education.
The gross insufficiency of midwifery and medical staff, and the limited functional health facilities severely limit access to quality maternal and child health care services, thus contributing to the high infant, child and maternal mortality rates.
Only 36.8% of pregnant women sought antenatal care between 3-6 months of their pregnancy, because of the lack of money or the non-existence of a health facility.  These conditions thus contribute to the high maternal mortality rate in Liberia, 578/100,000 (rural areas, 598/100,000 and urban, 381/100,000). Maternal mortality is primarily due to anemia, pastportum hemorrhage, sepsis, pregnancy-related complications, and toxemia and infections associated with abortions.
The overall low immunization level also explains the high infant mortality rate in Liberia, estimated as 117/1000 live birth. The major causes of infant and childhood mortality are malnutrition, neonatal tetanus, measles, acute respiratory infection (ARI), malaria and diarrhea. The immunization of children (age 12-23 months) against the childhood illnesses such as whooping cough, dipherria, tuberculosis, tetanus, poliomyellitis and measles is about 33%.  Immunization against polio has however increased due to the NID campaign.
A National Population Policy was developed with the objective to foster a balanced relationship between population and socio-economic growth, through the voluntary regulation of the fertility rate. A national plan of action was formulated covering the following major programs:  Maternal and child health, family planning and fertility regulations, IEC, the role and status of women, children and youth, and spatial distribution and urbanization.
HIV/AIDS prevalence is estimated at 8.2%, with an upward trend. The high incidence of poverty, and massive movement of people, both internally and externally, contributes to the development of the epidemy. Although 81% of the population of Liberia is aware of the existence of HIV/AIDS, the knowledge about the modes of transmission of HIV/AIDS has not reached most of the population, especially in the rural areas. Cultural practices such as traditional markings and FGM increase the risk of young people acquiring HIV/AIDS.  The potential for an upsurge in the prevalence of HIV/AIDS does exist, due to the disintegration of the institution of the family and the breakdown of the communities during the conflict.  Also, culturally the women lack control over their reproductive health, which make many of them susceptible to HIV/AIDS and other sexually transmitted diseases. 
Malaria is the leading cause of death in Liberia and accounts for over 40% of all cases dealt with in health facilities. Malaria prevalence has increased from 34.6 percent in 1997 to 50 percent in 1999-2000. The people at the highest risk to malaria are children under five, pregnant women, displaced populations and people with compromised immunity such as those with AIDS. The primary approach to malaria control should be early and correct treatment, the use of good quality ITNs, and the availability of good drugs at grass roots levels.
The government identified 9 priority diseases for Liberia: measles, bloody diarrhea, watery diarrhea, cholera, meningetis, yellow fever, lassa fever, Accute Flaccid Paralysis and Nio Natal Tetanos. The prevalence of some communicable diseases such as Tuberculosis, yellow fever, measles, meninginties are reaching alarming proportions. 
KEY CHALLENGES 
The main constraints facing Liberia in terms of prevention and control of diseases are the disruption of health services, poor knowledge of the diseases, poor access to health facilities, lack of laboratory, unavailability of drugs, suspected poor quality of drugs on the market place and inadequate manpower.

Working in partnership with the government, the National AIDS and STD Control Program (NACP) and NGOs, the UN Agencies have been supporting efforts aimed at controlling HIV/AIDS, malaria and priority diseases, through IEC and related activities, vulnerable group targeted workshops, health education, distribution of condoms, distribution of Insecticide Treated Nets (ITN), and youth education through the Ministry of Education. The UN System is also supporting the rehabilitation of health facilities and the provision of essential drugs, equipment and the training of health workers. The greatest area of success in the improvement of health care delivery system has been in the area of immunization under the National Immunization Days (NIDs), which is geared towards eradicating polio. The campaign provided 100 per cent coverage of children under-five years.
The UN System, particularly WHO, UNICEF, UNFPA and UNDP, will continue to assist the government in promoting and enhancing the quality of health. The UN system, with UNFPA taking the lead, will continue to work with the government and other bilateral and multilateral agencies to continue to promote reproductive health programmes with the view of improving life expectancy, family planning compliance, and reducing teenage pregnancies, maternal and infant mortality.

Objective 1: 	enhanced gender equity and women empowerment
Globally, there is mounting concern about the gender inequality and the low socio-economic status of women. Liberia faces major gender disparities, women’s access to health and education as well as to productive assets is still limited. Women constitute about half of the population and only 24% are literate, compared to 50% for males, 40% and 32% enrollments in primary and secondary school respectively, compared to 60% and 68% for males. There are also strong inequalities in terms of women’s participation in the public life and the decision-making processes, with only 11% of women participating in the national legislature.  
About 35% of household are headed by poor young women, which make them vulnerable and exposed to growing violence and HIV/AIDS. Over 80% of rural women depend on subsistence farming and play a major role in food production, processing and marketing. There are structural gender biases in the development process, which require the creation of an enabling environment and direct increase to women’s ability and quality of life. As farmers, Liberian women are custodians of the environment as they manage and preserve biodiversity. Women’s role in agriculture and in other aspects of rural sector has also an impact on food security.  Lastly, women have become persistent in search for peace and stability through national and regional initiatives, such as the Mano River Women Peace Network.

Objective 2: 		enhanced child protection and child development
Liberia has a relatively young population. The population is young, with approximately 48% being under 15 years. Children are very vulnerable. About 20% of children under 15 years of age live with neither biological parent. Infant mortality in Liberia is estimated at 117/1000 live birth. Children suffer of hunger and malnutrition. About 39M of children under five year of age are stunted, 6% thin and 26% underweight. The immunization of children (age 12-23 months) against the childhood illnesses such as whooping cough, dipherria, tuberculosis, tetanus, poliomyellitis and measles is about 33%.

Objective 3 : 	increased awareness on environmental and natural resources management 
Liberia has rich biodiversity with many natural resources that could contribute immensely to the socio-economic well being of the nation. About 43% of the Upper Guinea Forest is maintained by Liberia. Since the civil war, these resources are under increased pressure. Activities that are contributing to the destruction of the forests are excessive logging, farming and settlements. Charcoal and firewood are alternative means of energy. Huge urban migration is severely exerting pressure on limited resource and infrastructure. There is corresponding increase in unregulated waste dumped.  
In order to redress these environmental problems, the Government with the assistance of UNDP prepared Environmental Legislation, Policy and completed a State of the Environment. The Government has passed into law many of the Environmental Legislation, including the protocol on Wet-Land. Liberia asserts to the global protocols on the environment, including the convention to combat desertification, the convention on Biological Diversity and Agenda 21.  
The key challenges facing Liberia are uncoordinated distribution of tasks on environmental issues among various ministries/agencies, lack of public education and participation in the decision making process on the management of natural resources.

Part IV. Implementation Strategy, monitoring and follow up 
The UNDAF will serve as programming framework for all UN agencies and programmes in Liberia. Collaborative programming among the UN agencies encompasses options for parallel and joint programming. The strategic aim of such arrangements is to enhance development impact through the synergistic combination of inputs from two or more UN agencies. UN agencies have selected a number of areas where they will carry out joint assessment, and design programmes consisting of shared objectives, actions and timeframes with a clear delineation of responsibilities. These areas include: peace education and human rights, reintegration of ex-combatants, resettlement and reintegration of war affected populations, protection of refugees and IDPs, nutrition, gender equity and empowerment, immunization, fighting HIV/AIDS, roll back malaria.  
The UN agencies will ensure the alignment of their individual country programme with the objectives of the UNDAF. All UN agencies will have the responsibility of monitoring the implementation of the UNDAF through their periodic programme review. 
A UNDAF Task Force will be responsible for planning and managing the technical implementation of the UNDAF under the overall guidance of the UN Country Team.  Thematic groups will be a critical mechanism to plan, monitor and carry out initiatives proposed in the UNDAF, including proposals for parallel or joint programming. 
Under the overall guidance of the UNCT, the following monitoring and evaluations actions will be taken: 
The UNDAF Task Force will conduct an annual review of the UNDAF using the indicators set for each objective, in parallel with the preparation of the report on the Millennium Development Goals. Linkages will be made between the indicators established to measure the outputs of the UNDAF and the overall contribution of the UNDAF process to the national development objectives and the progress towards the Millennium Development Goals. 
The UN Country Team will organize a mid-term review of the UNDAF with the government and other development partners to review the achievement of the objectives, including the quality of partnership and collaborative programming. At the end of the UNDAF cycle, the UN Country Team will organize an evaluation of the UNDAF that will focus on lessons learned during the UNDAF implementation and assess the progress made towards achieving goals and objectives. The Country Team will report on the implementation of the UNDAF through the annual Resident Coordinator's Report.
